theme: The genealogy of Adam, life, death, and the promise preserved
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 5:1-32 slowly. Yes, this is a genealogy, and it may feel like one of those passages that’s tempting to skim. Don’t. Genealogies in Scripture are theological documents. As you read, notice the repeated phrase “and he died,” the curious exception in verse 24, and the way the chapter ends in suspense.
settingTheScene:
Yesterday we read about the first murder and the spread of sin from one generation to the next. Genesis 5 takes a step back and gives us the full genealogy of Adam through Noah, ten generations from creation to the flood. It is one of the most important genealogies in the Bible, and it sets up everything that comes next. This is also the first genealogy of Scripture, and it teaches us how to read all the ones that follow.

Genealogies are not filler. They are theological records. They tell us who is in the line of promise, how God’s faithfulness has been transmitted from generation to generation, and how the world fits together as one story. This genealogy in particular establishes that there is an unbroken line from Adam to Noah, that humanity has been multiplying across the earth, that death has been spreading along with humanity, and that one man in particular, Enoch, escaped death by walking with God.
observation: Verse 1 explicitly recalls Genesis 1:27: God “made him in the likeness of God. Male and female he created them, and he blessed them.” The image of God survived the Fall, humanity still bears it.

Adam’s first descendant is described differently from himself: “Adam … fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth.” The image of God is now mediated through fallen humanity.
Each generation follows a strict formula: [Name] lived X years, fathered [Son], lived Y more years, fathered other sons and daughters, and the years of his life were Z, AND HE DIED.
The phrase “and he died” appears eight times. Death, the consequence promised in Genesis 2:17, has come true and is now the universal human experience.
Enoch is the seventh from Adam and breaks the pattern. He “walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.” He does not die.

Lamech (a different Lamech than Cain’s descendant) names his son Noah, saying “this one shall give us rest from our work and from the painful toil of our hands because of the ground that the LORD has cursed.”
The genealogy ends not with “and he died” for Noah, but with the open-ended note that he “had three sons”, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. The story is not over yet.
interpretation:
Genesis 5 looks like a list, but it is preaching. The whole chapter is built around a tension: the image of God in humanity, and the reality of death that now follows every human life. Both are true. The chapter holds them together and lets us feel the weight.

Verse 1 deliberately echoes Genesis 1:27. “When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God. Male and female he created them, and he blessed them when they were created.” After the Fall and after Cain’s violence, the writer wants us to remember: humanity is still in the image of God. The Fall did not erase the image. It marred it, but it did not destroy it. Every person born to Adam and Eve, including Cain, bears the image of God. And this matters because the image will run through this chapter, generation by generation, all the way to Noah and beyond.

But then verse 3 introduces a haunting modification. Seth is born, and the text says Adam “fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image.” The phrase has shifted. Adam was made in God’s image; Seth is made in Adam’s image. The image is now mediated through fallen humanity. This is the doctrine of original sin being expressed not through theological argument but through narrative shading. The image survives. But it is now passed down through people who have already inherited the corruption of the Fall. Every child born is in the image of God and in the image of fallen Adam at the same time.

Then comes the repeated rhythm of the chapter: “and he died.” Eight times. Each life recorded, each life ended. The chapter is, in one sense, a long funeral. The promise of Genesis 2:17, “in the day you eat of it you shall surely die”, is being slowly, generation by generation, fulfilled. Death is not just an unfortunate biological fact; it is a theological reality. It is the consequence of sin. And it is now woven into the fabric of human existence.

This is what makes Enoch’s story so stunning. Verse 24: “Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.” Enoch is the seventh from Adam, and seven is the number of completeness, of fullness, and he breaks the pattern. He does not die. The text does not explain how or why, but the phrase “walked with God” appears only twice in the Old Testament about an individual: about Enoch here and about Noah in Genesis 6:9. The implication is clear: there is a kind of life that escapes the universal sentence of death. There is a way of relating to God that transforms what death does to a person. Hebrews 11:5 puts it this way: “By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death.” Enoch is the first hint in Scripture that death is not the final word, even though death has come for everyone else, there is one who walks with God and bypasses the grave entirely.

The chapter then comes to its climax with Lamech and Noah. Lamech names his son Noah, which sounds like the Hebrew word for “rest.” And he explains the name: “this one shall give us rest from our work and from the painful toil of our hands because of the ground that the LORD has cursed.” Lamech is reaching back to Genesis 3:17, where the ground was cursed because of Adam’s sin, and he is hoping, perhaps even prophesying, that this child will somehow lift the curse. He doesn’t fully grasp what he is saying. Noah will not lift the curse permanently. But Noah will be the means by which God preserves humanity through the flood, and through Noah’s line the true rest-giver will eventually come. The line of promise runs from Adam to Seth to Enosh to Enoch to Noah, and from there, all the way to Christ, who alone gives true rest to the weary.
connection: Yesterday’s reading showed sin spreading after the Fall, from Cain’s anger to Lamech’s vengeance. Today’s chapter shows the bigger picture: ten generations of human history, with death claiming each one in turn. This is the world that the gospel will eventually answer. The promise of Genesis 3:15 (the offspring of the woman) is being preserved through a particular family line, Seth, Enosh, and onward to Noah, and ultimately to Abraham and David and Christ. Enoch’s escape from death foreshadows the resurrection. Lamech’s hope for rest through Noah foreshadows the deeper rest we have in Jesus. Even a genealogy is gospel-shaped when you know how to read it.
application:
The repeated phrase “and he died” is meant to land on you. Every human life that has ever been lived will end with that phrase. Yours will too. The Bible does not let you forget this, because pretending death is not coming is one of the most spiritually corrosive habits a human can have. Death is real. It is the consequence of sin. And it will claim you.

But Enoch is in this chapter for a reason. Enoch walked with God, and death did not have its way with him. The Christian message is not that death is unreal or that we should be brave about it. The Christian message is that death has been conquered by the one who walked with God perfectly, Jesus, and that those who are in him will follow him through death into life. Hebrews 11 lists Enoch among the heroes of faith because his story is a sign: there is a way of relating to God that changes what death does to you.

Today, ask yourself: am I walking with God? Not perfectly, Enoch alone is described that way among ordinary humans, but truly. Is my life a daily walk with the God who made me, redeemed me, and is sanctifying me? Or have I drifted into a religious routine that does not feel like walking with anyone? The phrase “walked with God” appears precious few times in Scripture. It is offered to you. Take it up.

And if you have lost someone, or are afraid of losing someone, or are afraid of your own death, let Genesis 5 do its work in two directions. Yes, death is real. Yes, it is coming. But the same chapter that records death also records Enoch, who walked with God and was taken. In Christ, that is the trajectory of every believer.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that his image still marks you, and tell him how you feel when you think about death.
Ask him to help you walk with him as Enoch did, day by day.
Thank Christ that death is not the end for those who are his.
